claim: CD8+ T cell anergy is a critical mechanism of peripheral tolerance.
source: CD8+ T cell anergy is a critical mechanism of peripheral tolerance, poorly investigated in response to immunotherapy.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract presenting established knowledge in the field.

claim: Intragraft CD8+ lymphocytes coexpressing granzyme B and perforin were selectively depleted through the Fas/FasL pathway after CD3 antibody therapy.
source: using a pancreatic islet allograft model and CD3 antibody therapy, we showed, by single cell gene profiling, that intragraft CD8+ lymphocytes coexpressing granzyme B and perforin were selectively depleted through the Fas/FasL pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by single cell gene profiling data presented in the manuscript showing selective depletion of Gzmb+Prf1+ cells.

claim: Selective depletion of Gzmb+Prf1+ CD8+ T cells led to long-standing anergy of the remaining CD8+ T cells.
source: This step led to long-standing anergy of the remaining CD8+ T cells marked by the absence of cytotoxic/inflammatory gene expression also confirmed by transcriptome analysis.
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR and transcriptome analysis data showing absence of cytotoxic/inflammatory gene expression.

claim: Sustained unresponsiveness of CD8+ T cells required the presence of alloantigens.
source: This sustained unresponsiveness required the presence of the alloantigens.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments showing that islet allografts transplanted 2 months after CD8+ T cell transfer were rejected.

claim: Tissue-resident CD8+ lymphocytes produced TGFβ after CD3 antibody treatment.
source: Furthermore, tissue-resident CD8+ lymphocytes produced TGFβ and expressed the inhibitory receptors PD-1 and PD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data showing Tgfb1 mRNA expression in 65% of intragraft CD8+ T cells.

claim: Tissue-resident CD8+ lymphocytes expressed the inhibitory receptors PD-1 and PD-L1 after CD3 antibody treatment.
source: Furthermore, tissue-resident CD8+ lymphocytes produced TGFβ and expressed the inhibitory receptors PD-1 and PD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing upregulation of PD-1 and PD-L1 on intragraft CD8+ T cells.

claim: Blockade of TGFβ downregulated PD-1 and PD-L1 expression and precipitated graft rejection.
source: Blockade of TGFβ downregulated PD-1 and PD-L1 expression and precipitated graft rejection.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments showing that neutralizing TGFβ antibodies reduced PD-1/PD-L1 expression and abrogated tolerance.

claim: Neutralizing PD-1 signaling abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
source: Neutralizing PD-1, PD-L1 or TGFβRII signaling in T cells also abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data showing rejection when anti-PD-1 antibodies were administered with CD3 antibodies.

claim: Neutralizing PD-L1 signaling abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
source: Neutralizing PD-1, PD-L1 or TGFβRII signaling in T cells also abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data showing rejection when anti-PD-L1 antibodies were administered with CD3 antibodies.

claim: Neutralizing TGFβRII signaling in T cells abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
source: Neutralizing PD-1, PD-L1 or TGFβRII signaling in T cells also abrogated CD3 antibody-induced tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data showing rejection in DnTGFβRII transgenic mice treated with CD3 antibodies.

claim: There is a cell intrinsic regulatory link between the TGFβ and the PD-1/PD-L1 pathways.
source: These studies unravel novel mechanisms underlying CD8+ T cell anergy and reveal a cell intrinsic regulatory link between the TGFβ and the PD-1/PD-L1 pathways.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that TGFβ blockade downregulates PD-1/PD-L1 expression and that TGFβRII signaling in T cells is required for tolerance.

claim: CD8+ T cells play a major role in transplant rejection.
source: CD8+ T cells play major role in transplant rejection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the transplantation field.

claim: CD8+ T cells get activated by donor antigen-presenting cells through direct presentation.
source: Through direct presentation, they get activated by donor antigen-presenting cells (APC), in particular dendritic cells, which migrate from the graft to secondary lymphoid organs (Gras et al., 2011; Ochando et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Direct presentation of donor antigens induces rapid, intense responses that cause acute graft rejection.
source: This response is rapid, intense and induces acute graft rejection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about direct allorecognition.

claim: Recipient APC capture donor antigens from the transplant and present them to alloreactive CD8+ T cells through self MHC I molecules.
source: Recipient APC also capture donor antigens from the transplant, present them to alloreactive CD8+ T cells through self MHC I molecules (cross-priming/indirect presentation) hereby contributing to acute and chronic graft rejection (Celli et al., 2011; Valujskikh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes migrate to the graft where they destroy target cells through granzyme B/perforin- and/or Fas/FasLigand-dependent cytolytic pathways.
source: Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes migrate to the graft where they destroy target cells through granzyme B/perforin- and/or Fas/FasLigand-dependent cytolytic pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD8+ T cell cytotoxic mechanisms.

claim: Long-term graft survival was associated with CD8+ T cell dysfunction in most tolerance promoting protocols.
source: In most tolerance promoting protocols, long-term graft survival was associated with CD8+ T cell dysfunction which mainly resulted from clonal deletion and/or anergy (Iwakoshi et al., 2000; Monk et al., 2003; Qian et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Anergy is classically defined as the functional inactivation of T cells to cognate antigens.
source: Classically defined as the functional inactivation of T cells to cognate antigens, anergy was first described in vitro when T cells recognized antigens (signal 1) in absence of appropriate costimulation (signal 2), usually provided by CD28 (Schwartz, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Anergic T cells are not able to produce IL-2 and enter a hyporesponsive non proliferative state.
source: T cells were not able to produce IL-2, entered a hyporesponsive non proliferative state that prevented further responses upon antigen re-encounter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about anergic T cells.

claim: The transcription factors NF-AT and Egr-2/Egr-3 play a role in signaling events leading to anergy.
source: Over the last decade, better insight was gained into the signaling events leading to anergy, highlighting in particular the role of the transcription factors NF-AT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) and early growth response gene 2 and 3 (Egr-2, Egr-3) (Macian et al., 2002; Safford et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD3 antibodies induced tolerance in fully MHC-mismatched experimental models of pancreatic islet and cardiac transplantation.
source: Recently, we reported that CD3 antibodies (CD3 Abs) induced tolerance in fully MHC-mismatched experimental models of pancreatic islet and cardiac transplantation (Goto et al., 2013; You et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Long-term graft acceptance with CD3 antibodies was obtained only when treatment was administered a few days post-transplant after T cell priming had occurred.
source: The timing of treatment was crucial; long-term graft acceptance was obtained only when CD3 Abs were administered once T cell priming had occurred, a few days post-transplant.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies by the authors.

claim: Permanent survival of a second graft from the original donor but not from third-party donor demonstrated that antigen-specific tolerance had been induced.
source: Permanent survival of a second graft from the original donor but not from third-party donor demonstrated that antigen-specific tolerance had been induced.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies by the authors.

claim: Purified spleen CD8+ T cells from CD3 Ab-treated recipients were unable to respond when stimulated with donor antigens while response to third-party antigens was conserved.
source: Purified spleen CD8+ T cells from CD3 Ab-treated recipients were unable to respond when stimulated with donor antigens while response to third-party antigens was conserved (You et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: CD3 Abs preferentially targeted and depleted activated effector T cells, notably within the graft.
source: In this model, CD3 Abs preferentially targeted and depleted activated effector T cells, notably within the graft.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies by the authors.

claim: Intragraft T cells recovered after CD3 Ab treatment did not respond to BALB/c donor antigens.
source: Intragraft T cells recovered after CD3 Ab treatment, on days 14 or 100 post-transplant, did not respond to BALB/c donor antigens as opposed to graft infiltrating T cells of untreated recipients analyzed few days before rejection (day 14) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by IFNγ Elispot assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: On day 14 post-transplant in untreated recipients, graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells expressed the cytolytic molecules Gzmb, Prf1 and Fasl as well as Tbx21 and Klrg1.
source: On day 14 post-transplant, in untreated recipients, graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells expressed the cytolytic molecules Gzmb, Prf1 and Fasl as well as Tbx21 and Klrg1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Thirty three percent of graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells in untreated recipients co-expressed 3 or more of the 7 genes tested on day 14 post-transplant.
source: Thirty three percent of these cells co-expressed 3 or more of the 7 genes tested (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gzmb was co-expressed with either Prf1 or Fasl which rarely overlapped in untreated recipients.
source: Interestingly, Gzmb was co-expressed with either Prf1 or Fasl which rarely overlapped, suggesting the presence of two distinct subsets of graft infiltrating CD8+ lymphocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There are two distinct subsets of graft infiltrating CD8+ lymphocytes in untreated recipients.
source: Interestingly, Gzmb was co-expressed with either Prf1 or Fasl which rarely overlapped, suggesting the presence of two distinct subsets of graft infiltrating CD8+ lymphocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutually exclusive expression patterns of Prf1 and Fasl with Gzmb.

claim: Tbx21, Eomes and Klrg1 were preferentially associated with Prf1 rather than Fasl in untreated recipients.
source: Tbx21, Eomes and Klrg1 were preferentially associated with Prf1 rather than Fasl (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In CD3 Ab-treated recipients on day +14, expression of Prf1, Tbx21, Klrg1 and Gzmb by intragraft CD8+ T cells was clearly reduced as compared to untreated mice.
source: In CD3 Ab-treated recipients, on day +14 after transplantation, expression of Prf1, Tbx21, Klrg1 and Gzmb by intragraft CD8+ T cells was clearly reduced as compared to untreated mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The frequency of intragraft CD8+ T cells coexpressing 3 or more genes was significantly decreased after CD3 Ab treatment (from 33.3% to 15.3%).
source: The frequency of cells coexpressing 3 or more genes was significantly decreased (from 33.3% to 15.3%) while the number of cells expressing only one gene doubled after CD3 Ab treatment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A dramatic decrease in Gzmb+Prf1+ CD8+ T cells was observed after CD3 Ab treatment.
source: A dramatic decrease in Gzmb+Prf1+ CD8+ T cells was observed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Fasl expression was enhanced in intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab treatment (50% versus 30.6% in untreated controls).
source: Contrasting with these findings, Fasl expression was enhanced as compared to untreated controls (50% versus 30.6%).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data.

claim: The increased FasL expression on intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab treatment was confirmed by flow cytometry.
source: The increased FasL expression on intragraft CD8+ T cells was confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Among the Fasl+ subset after CD3 Ab treatment, 38% co-expressed Gzmb (versus 62% in untreated recipients).
source: Among this Fasl+ subset, 38% co-expressed Gzmb (versus 62% in untreated recipients) and 33.3% did not express any other effector genes.
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data.

claim: On day 100 post-transplant, expression of Fasl, Prf1, Tbx21 and Eomes was detected in less than 5% of intragraft CD8+ T cells in CD3 Ab-treated tolerant mice.
source: On day 100 post-transplant, expression of Fasl, Prf1, Tbx21 and Eomes was detected in less than 5% of intragraft CD8+ T cells in CD3 Ab-treated tolerant mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Only 5.6% of intragraft CD8+ T cells coexpressed 3 or more genes on day 100 post-transplant in CD3 Ab-treated mice.
source: Only 5.6% of CD8+ T cells coexpressed 3 or more genes and 43.1% of the cells did not express any of the 7 inflammatory/cytotoxic genes tested (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Gzmb was detected in 26% of intragraft CD8+ T cells on day 100 but was not associated with Fasl or Prf1.
source: Gzmb was detected in 26% of the cells but was not associated with Fasl or Prf1 suggesting the absence of potent cytotoxic function (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The absence of Gzmb association with Fasl or Prf1 suggests the absence of potent cytotoxic function.
source: Gzmb was detected in 26% of the cells but was not associated with Fasl or Prf1 suggesting the absence of potent cytotoxic function (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of co-expression of cytotoxic effector molecules.

claim: In the spleen, a large proportion (56%) of CD8+ T cells from untreated mice coexpressed Gzmb, Tbx21 and Klrg1 but not Prf1 or Fasl on day +14 post-transplant.
source: In the spleen, the single cell gene profile differed from that of intragraft T cells. A large proportion (56%) of CD8+ T cells from untreated mice coexpressed Gzmb, Tbx21 and Klrg1 but nor Prf1 or Fasl on day +14 post-transplant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: After CD3 Ab therapy, 52% and 37.5% of spleen CD8+ T cells expressed none or only one of the 7 selected genes, respectively.
source: Such coexpression was abrogated after CD3 Ab therapy as 52% and 37.5% of spleen CD8+ T cells expressed none or only one of the 7 selected genes, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by single cell PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and 2C.

claim: RT-qPCR on total islet allografts confirmed the decreased expression of Gzmb, Prf1, Tbx21 and Ifng after CD3 Ab treatment.
source: RT-qPCR on total islet allografts confirmed the decreased expression of Gzmb, Prf1, Tbx21 and Ifng (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Fasl expression was reduced on day +14 post-transplant by RT-qPCR, which contrasts with single cell PCR results.
source: Fasl expression was also reduced on day +14 post-transplant which contrasts with results from single cell PCR (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Fas mRNA expression increased after administration of CD3 Abs on day +14 post-transplant and decreased thereafter.
source: We also analyzed expression of Fas mRNA which, interestingly, increased after administration of CD3 Abs on day +14 post-transplant and decreased hereafter.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: CD3 Abs rapidly induced Fas expression on CD8+ T cells after a 24 hr in vitro stimulation.
source: We confirmed by flow cytometry that CD3 Abs rapidly induced Fas expression on CD8+ T cells after a 24 hr in vitro stimulation and most of them co-expressed FasL at 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Most CD8+ T cells co-expressed FasL at 48 hr after in vitro stimulation with CD3 Abs.
source: We confirmed by flow cytometry that CD3 Abs rapidly induced Fas expression on CD8+ T cells after a 24 hr in vitro stimulation and most of them co-expressed FasL at 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Long-term islet allograft survival was not observed when FasL was blocked during CD3 Ab therapy.
source: To investigate whether CD3 Ab-induced depletion of alloreactive CD8+ T cells was dependent on the Fas/FasL pathway, monoclonal antibodies neutralizing FasL were administered in C57BL/6 recipients at the time of CD3 Ab therapy. Long-term islet allograft survival was not observed in this condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FasL blockade abrogated CD3 Ab depleting effect on CD8+ T cells.
source: FasL blockade abrogated CD3 Ab depleting effect: CD8+ T cells were detected within the islet allografts at levels comparable to that found in untreated recipients (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FasL expression was drastically reduced on infiltrating CD8+ T cells when FasL was blocked during CD3 Ab therapy.
source: FasL expression was drastically reduced on infiltrating CD8+ T cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab treatment were CD69+ CD44highCD62LlowCD45RBlow on day 14 post-transplant.
source: On day 14 post-transplant, most of them were CD69+ CD44highCD62LlowCD45RBlow (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab treatment expressed low levels of CD122 and CD25 as opposed to intragraft CD8+ T cells from untreated mice.
source: They expressed low levels of CD122 (the β subunit of the IL-2 and IL-15 receptors) and CD25 as opposed to intragraft CD8+ T cells from untreated mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of the proliferation marker Ki67 was strongly reduced after CD3 Ab therapy.
source: Expression of the proliferation marker Ki67 was also strongly reduced after CD3 Ab therapy.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The inhibitory receptors PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG3 were upregulated on intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab therapy.
source: In contrast, the inhibitory receptors PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG3 were upregulated (58.5%, 60.9% and 58.6% versus 25%, 26.1% and 27% without treatment, respectively) and were mostly co-expressed by the same cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG3 were mostly co-expressed by the same intragraft CD8+ T cells after CD3 Ab therapy.
source: In contrast, the inhibitory receptors PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG3 were upregulated (58.5%, 60.9% and 58.6% versus 25%, 26.1% and 27% without treatment, respectively) and were mostly co-expressed by the same cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: A large proportion of intragraft CD8+ T cells still expressed inhibitory receptors on day +100 post-transplant.
source: This phenotype was maintained over long-term since a large proportion of intragraft CD8+ T cells still expressed these inhibitory receptors on day +100 post-transplant.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: CD8+ T cells in the spleen and draining lymph nodes showed an increase in PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG-3 expression after CD3 Ab therapy.
source: A similar trend was observed in the spleen and draining lymph nodes where CD8+ T cells showed an increase in PD-1, PD-L1 and LAG-3 expression after CD3 Ab therapy (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD3 antibody-induced upregulation of PD-L1 on intragraft CD8+ T cells was inhibited following in vivo FasL blockade.
source: Interestingly, CD3 antibody-induced upregulation of PD-L1 on intragraft CD8+ T cells was inhibited following in vivo FasL blockade (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of CD25 and T-bet were significantly increased in recipients treated with the combination of CD3 and FasL Abs as compared to CD3 Abs alone.
source: In addition, expression of CD25 and T-bet were significantly increased in recipients treated with the combination of CD3 and FasL Abs as compared to CD3 Abs alone, reaching levels similar to those observed in untreated mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Recipients rejected their graft when treated with CD3 Abs together with anti-PD-1 antibodies (median survival of 33.7 ± 1.5 days).
source: To investigate the role of the PD-1/PDL-1 pathway in CD3 Ab-induced transplant tolerance, we treated C57BL/6 mice at day 7 with CD3 Abs together with monoclonal Abs to PD-1 or PD-L1. In both cases, recipients rejected their graft with a median survival of 33.7 ± 1.5 days or 28.6 ± 5.1 days, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Recipients rejected their graft when treated with CD3 Abs together with anti-PD-L1 antibodies (median survival of 28.6 ± 5.1 days).
source: To investigate the role of the PD-1/PDL-1 pathway in CD3 Ab-induced transplant tolerance, we treated C57BL/6 mice at day 7 with CD3 Abs together with monoclonal Abs to PD-1 or PD-L1. In both cases, recipients rejected their graft with a median survival of 33.7 ± 1.5 days or 28.6 ± 5.1 days, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After administration of PD-1 Abs, most graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells were CD44highCD62LlowTbet+ and strongly proliferated.
source: After administration of PD-1 Abs, most graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells were CD44highCD62LlowTbet+ and strongly proliferated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Blockade of PD-L1 at the time of established tolerance (day 100) precipitated graft rejection.
source: Anti-PD-L1 Abs were also injected in tolerant recipients, on day 100 after transplantation and CD3 Ab therapy. Blockade of PD-L1 at the time of established tolerance precipitated graft rejection (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Islet grafts survived when purified spleen CD8+ T cells from CD3 Ab-treated tolerant mice were transferred into RAG-/- recipients transplanted on the same day with BALB/c pancreatic islets.
source: To further dissect the role of this pathway in CD8+ T cell tolerance, we adoptively transferred purified spleen CD8+ T cells from CD3 Ab-treated tolerant mice into immunodeficient RAG-/- recipients transplanted on the same day with BALB/c pancreatic islets. Islet grafts survived in these recipients.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data.

claim: Transferred CD8+ T cells from tolerant mice were detected in significant proportion in the spleen, draining lymph nodes and within recipients' transplants.
source: Transferred CD8+ T cells were detected in significant proportion in the spleen, draining lymph nodes and within recipients' transplants (Figure 4D–E)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Transferred tolerant CD8+ T cells stained CD44high but did not produce high amounts of IFNγ in response to PMA/ionomycin stimulation.
source: they stained CD44high but did not produce high amounts of IFNγ in response to PMA/ionomycin stimulation (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Administration of PD-L1 Abs on day +100 post-transplant in RAG-/- recipients that received tolerant CD8+ T cells provoked graft rejection.
source: Administration of PD-L1 Abs on day +100 post-transplant provoked graft rejection (Figure 4C) and restored the capacity of CD8+ T cells to secrete IFNγ (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C, 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Administration of PD-L1 Abs restored the capacity of tolerant CD8+ T cells to secrete IFNγ.
source: Administration of PD-L1 Abs on day +100 post-transplant provoked graft rejection (Figure 4C) and restored the capacity of CD8+ T cells to secrete IFNγ (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All grafts were rejected when RAG-/- recipients were grafted with BALB/c pancreatic islets more than two months after transfer of purified CD8+ T cells from tolerant mice.
source: To assess the role of donor alloantigens in sustaining CD8+ T cell unresponsiveness, RAG-/- C57BL/6 recipients were grafted under the kidney capsule with BALB/c pancreatic islets either on the same day or more than two months after transfer of purified CD8+ T cells recovered from tolerant mice, to exclude any impact of homeostatic proliferation on T cell functional properties. In this later condition, all grafts were rejected contrasting with the long-term survival obtained when cell transfer and islet grafts were both performed on day 0. (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A 4-week interval between infusion of tolerant CD8+ T cells and islet allografts also led to graft rejection.
source: A 4-week interval between infusion of tolerant CD8+ T cells and islet allografts also led to graft rejection (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Control syngeneic islet grafts were tolerated in RAG-/- recipients that received tolerant CD8+ T cells.
source: Control syngeneic islet grafts were tolerated.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data.

claim: RT-qPCR results on islet grafts recovered from CD3 Ab-treated recipients showed a significant increase of Tgfb1 mRNA, as compared to untreated controls.
source: RT-qPCR results on islet grafts recovered from CD3 Ab-treated recipients showed a significant increase of Tgfb1 mRNA, as compared to untreated controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The intragraft Tgfb1/Ifng ratio was increased over long-term after CD3 Ab treatment.
source: In addition, the intragraft Tgfb1/Ifng ratio was increased over long-term.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Tgfb1 mRNA was expressed in 52% and 65% of CD4+ and CD8+ intragraft T cells, respectively, after CD3 Ab treatment.
source: To further identify the source of TGFβ, we sorted individual T lymphocytes, recovered on day 14 post-transplant, either from the spleen or from the islet grafts of 3 recipient mice treated with CD3 Abs. Expression of Tgfb1 mRNA was determined by single cell qPCR on 60 CD8+ and 48 CD4+ T cells. Results showed that Tgfb1 mRNA was expressed in 52% and 65% of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by single cell qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In untreated recipients, only 9% of CD4+ and 6% of CD8+ intragraft T cells expressed Tgfb1.
source: In untreated recipients, only 9% of CD4+ and 6% of CD8+ intragraft T cells expressed Tgfb1.
evidence: This is supported by single cell qPCR data.

claim: Tgfb1 mRNA was expressed in very few T cells recovered from the spleen of untreated or CD3 Ab-treated mice.
source: Tgfb1 mRNA was expressed in very few T cells recovered from the spleen of the same untreated or CD3 Ab-treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by single cell qPCR data.

claim: Administration of a neutralizing antibody to TGFβ partially, yet significantly, abrogated CD3 Ab-induced tolerance.
source: Administration of a neutralizing antibody to TGFβ partially, yet significantly, abrogated CD3 Ab-induced tolerance (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment of DnTGFβRII transgenic recipients with CD3 Ab on day +7 post-transplant did not induce long-term survival of islet allografts (median survival of 36.8 ± 6.1 days).
source: To assess whether TGFβ signaling within T cells was involved in the effect observed, we used as recipients transgenic DnTGFβRII C57BL/6 mice that express a dominant negative form of the human TGFβ receptor II under the control of the mouse CD4 promoter (Gorelik and Flavell, 2000). In these mice, the dnTGFBRII-CD4 transgenic construct lacks the CD8 silencer. Thus, expression of the transgene blocks TGFβ signaling specifically in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Treatment of these transgenic recipients with CD3 Ab on day +7 post-transplant did not induce long-term survival of islet allografts (median survival of 36.8 ± 6.1 days) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Co-expression of PD-1 and PD-L1 was induced after TCR stimulation in vitro.
source: T cells were stimulated in vitro for 24 hr with CD3 Abs in presence of neutralizing Abs to TGFβ or recombinant TGFβ. Co-expression of PD-1 and PD-L1 was induced after TCR stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blockade of TGFβ downregulated expression of PD-1 and even more drastically that of PD-L1 in vitro.
source: Blockade of TGFβ downregulated expression of PD-1 and even more drastically that of PD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro flow cytometry data.

claim: Addition of recombinant TGFβ to the culture further promoted PD-1 but not PD-L1 expression in vitro.
source: In contrast, addition of recombinant TGFβ to the culture further promoted PD-1 but not PD-L1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro flow cytometry data.

claim: In vivo neutralization of TGFβ downregulated PD-1 and PD-L1 co-expression on graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells.
source: To assess the relevance of this pathway in vivo, islet allograft recipients were treated with CD3 Abs either alone or combined with TGFβ Abs. Paralleling the in vitro data, in vivo neutralization of TGFβ downregulated PD-1 and PD-L1 co-expression on graft infiltrating CD8+ T cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Gene categories related to effective T cell responses were downregulated in CD3 Ab treated mice as compared to controls.
source: Using the Agilent platform, we compared intragraft CD8+ T cells from CD3 Ab-treated tolerant mice to those from untreated mice showing acute rejection. Functional grouping analysis showed that gene categories related to effective T cell responses were downregulated in CD3 Ab treated mice as compared to controls (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Pathways induced by IL-2 or TCR signaling were downregulated in CD3 Ab treated mice.
source: Accordingly, pathways induced by IL-2 or TCR signaling were also downregulated (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44).
source: Analysis of immune genes differentially expressed between the two groups revealed a decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44), proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1), co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4), inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21) and environmental sensing (hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed decreased expression of genes involved in proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1).
source: Analysis of immune genes differentially expressed between the two groups revealed a decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44), proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1), co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4), inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21) and environmental sensing (hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed decreased expression of genes involved in co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4).
source: Analysis of immune genes differentially expressed between the two groups revealed a decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44), proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1), co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4), inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21) and environmental sensing (hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed decreased expression of genes involved in inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21).
source: Analysis of immune genes differentially expressed between the two groups revealed a decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44), proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1), co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4), inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21) and environmental sensing (hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed decreased expression of the hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a.
source: Analysis of immune genes differentially expressed between the two groups revealed a decreased expression of genes involved in cell migration (Cxcl9, Ccr10, Nrp1, Cd44), proliferation (Fos, Jun, Ccnd1), co-stimulation (Cd80, Icos, Cd200, Ctla4), inflammatory cytokine signaling (Tnf, Il2ra, Il1r2, Il18r1, Tnfrsf21) and environmental sensing (hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In tolerant CD8+ T cells, categories related to metabolic processes (nucleotides, energy, carbohydrates, lipids) were enriched.
source: In tolerant CD8+ T cells, categories related to metabolic processes (nucleotides, energy, carbohydrates, lipids…) as well as cell cycle arrest were enriched.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data.

claim: In tolerant CD8+ T cells, categories related to cell cycle arrest were enriched.
source: In tolerant CD8+ T cells, categories related to metabolic processes (nucleotides, energy, carbohydrates, lipids…) as well as cell cycle arrest were enriched.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed upregulation of genes inhibiting or regulating T cell functions: inhibitors of cell proliferation (Hopx, Cdkn2c, Map2k6, Mapk9).
source: In addition, these cells showed upregulation of genes inhibiting or regulating T cell functions: inhibitors of cell proliferation (Hopx, Cdkn2c, Map2k6, Mapk9), of cytokine signaling (Socs2, Socs6), of differentiation (Eid2, Id2), of co-stimulation (Btla) (Figure 8C and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed upregulation of inhibitors of cytokine signaling (Socs2, Socs6).
source: In addition, these cells showed upregulation of genes inhibiting or regulating T cell functions: inhibitors of cell proliferation (Hopx, Cdkn2c, Map2k6, Mapk9), of cytokine signaling (Socs2, Socs6), of differentiation (Eid2, Id2), of co-stimulation (Btla) (Figure 8C and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed upregulation of inhibitors of differentiation (Eid2, Id2).
source: In addition, these cells showed upregulation of genes inhibiting or regulating T cell functions: inhibitors of cell proliferation (Hopx, Cdkn2c, Map2k6, Mapk9), of cytokine signaling (Socs2, Socs6), of differentiation (Eid2, Id2), of co-stimulation (Btla) (Figure 8C and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tolerant CD8+ T cells showed upregulation of inhibitors of co-stimulation (Btla).
source: In addition, these cells showed upregulation of genes inhibiting or regulating T cell functions: inhibitors of cell proliferation (Hopx, Cdkn2c, Map2k6, Mapk9), of cytokine signaling (Socs2, Socs6), of differentiation (Eid2, Id2), of co-stimulation (Btla) (Figure 8C and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Eomes, encoding for the IFNγ transcription factor eomesodermin, was upregulated in tolerant CD8 T cells.
source: Eomes, encoding for the IFNγ transcription factor eomesodermin, was also upregulated in tolerant CD8 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data.

claim: CD3 Abs selectively deplete graft-infiltrating Gzmb+Prf1+ cytotoxic CD8+ T cells by a FasL-mediated pathway.
source: In the present study, using a pancreatic islet allograft model and CD3 Ab therapy, we provide novel insights into the immune mechanisms driving and sustaining CD8+ T cell anergy thus leading to long-term graft survival. We demonstrate that CD3 Abs selectively deplete graft-infiltrating Gzmb+Prf1+ cytotoxic CD8+ T cells by a FasL-mediated pathway.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulatory and effector T cells were differentially affected by CD3 Ab treatment.
source: We previously reported that a short-term course with CD3 Abs induced long-term graft survival and antigen-specific tolerance provided the treatment was applied in a defined therapeutic window, that is at the time of effector T cells priming to the alloantigens (Goto et al., 2013; You et al., 2012). Mechanistic studies revealed that regulatory and effector T cells were differentially affected by the treatment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Foxp3 Tregs were relatively spared from CD3 Ab-induced depletion and could transfer antigen-specific tolerance.
source: Foxp3 Tregs were relatively spared from CD3 Ab-induced depletion and could transfer antigen-specific tolerance, suggesting that they play an important role in sustaining graft survival (Baas et al., 2013; Goto et al., 2013; You et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: CD3 Abs preferentially induced apoptosis of activated effector T cells.
source: In contrast to Tregs, CD3 Abs preferentially induced apoptosis of activated effector T cells (You et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Long-term graft survival correlated with an absence of donor-specific CD8+ T cell responses at the periphery.
source: Long-term graft survival correlated with an absence of donor-specific CD8+ T cell responses at the periphery (You et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The IFNγ, perforin and Fas/FasL pathways constituted predominant mechanisms of CD8+ T cell-mediated destruction of islet allografts.
source: We focused our analysis on Th1 and cytotoxic genes as it has been shown that the IFNγ, perforin and Fas/FasL pathways constituted predominant mechanisms of CD8+ T cell-mediated destruction of islet allografts (Diamond and Gill, 2000; Sleater et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Signaling through the TCR/CD3 complex promotes activation-induced cell death (AICD) in activated effector T cells through a Fas/FasL interaction, but independently of perforin and granzymes.
source: Previous studies showed that signaling through the TCR/CD3 complex promotes activation-induced cell death (AICD) in activated effector T cells through a Fas/FasL interaction, but independently of perforin and granzymes (Brunner et al., 1995; Sobek et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apoptosis has occurred by triggering of Fas by FasL-expressing neighboring T cells.
source: Our results suggest, together with previous reports using T cell hybridomas or clones, that apoptosis has occurred by triggering of Fas by FasL-expressing neighboring T cells (Ayroldi et al., 1997; Brunner et al., 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing both Fas and FasL expression on T cells after CD3 Ab treatment, supported by citations.

claim: The remaining transgenic CD8+ T cells after AICD were intrinsically unresponsive to TCR stimuli.
source: The remaining transgenic CD8+ T cells were intrinsically unresponsive to TCR stimuli (Rocha and von Boehmer, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When HY-specific CD8+ T cells were parked into a second female nude recipient for 2 months and subsequently transferred into a third male nude mice, the T cells regained their ability to respond to the HY antigen.
source: Importantly, when parked into a second female nude recipient for 2 months and subsequently transferred into a third male nude mice, the T cells regained their ability to respond to the HY antigen showing that antigen persistence was required to maintain CD8 T cell anergy (Rocha et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Antigen persistence was required to maintain CD8 T cell anergy in the HY model.
source: Importantly, when parked into a second female nude recipient for 2 months and subsequently transferred into a third male nude mice, the T cells regained their ability to respond to the HY antigen showing that antigen persistence was required to maintain CD8 T cell anergy (Rocha et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Within islet allografts, chronic antigen encounter induces a suboptimal activation that reinforces anergic signals in CD8+ T cells and therefore sustains CD8 T cell tolerance.
source: Our data suggest that, within islet allografts, chronic antigen encounter induces a suboptimal activation that reinforces anergic signals in CD8+ T cells and therefore sustains CD8 T cell tolerance.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that continuous presence of alloantigen is required for maintaining CD8+ T cell unresponsiveness.

claim: Hopx (homeodomain-only protein) is a master regulator of the anergic state of induced Tregs.
source: Hopx (homeodomain-only protein), identified as a master regulator of the anergic state of induced Tregs, inhibits the expression of the AP-1 complex (Hawiger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fos and Jun compose the AP-1 complex.
source: Accordingly, Fos and Jun that compose the AP-1 complex were downregulated in tolerant CD8+ T cells as well as their downstream target cyclin D1 (Ccnd1) (Kang et al., 1992; Sundstedt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cyclin D1 (Ccnd1) is a downstream target of the AP-1 complex.
source: Accordingly, Fos and Jun that compose the AP-1 complex were downregulated in tolerant CD8+ T cells as well as their downstream target cyclin D1 (Ccnd1) (Kang et al., 1992; Sundstedt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cxcl9 encodes an IFNγ inducible chemokine contributing to the recruitment of allograft reactive T cells.
source: Additionally, the decreased expression of Cxcl9, encoding an IFNγ inducible chemokine contributing to the recruitment of allograft reactive T cells (Medoff et al., 2006), as well as that of Tnf, Il2ra, Lgals3, Il1r2, Il18r1 and Tnfrsf9 revealed the inhibition of Th1 inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hif1a positively regulates T cell differentiation and effector functions by promoting aerobic glycolysis.
source: Tolerant CD8+ T cells also downregulated the hypoxia-inducible factor Hif1a that has been shown to positively regulate T cell differentiation and effector functions by promoting aerobic glycolysis (Doedens et al., 2013; Finlay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eomesodermin (Eomes) plays well-described roles in cytotoxic CD8+ T cell differentiation and memory formation.
source: This was unexpected as eomesodermin (Eomes) plays well-described roles in cytotoxic CD8+ T cell differentiation and memory formation (Intlekofer et al., 2005; Pearce et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of Eomes by virus-specific CD8 T cells was associated with high expression of inhibitory receptors and impaired functions in models of chronic infections.
source: However, investigations in models of chronic infections in human and mouse (HIV, LCMV) have demonstrated that expression of Eomes by virus-specific CD8 T cells was associated with high expression of inhibitory receptors and impaired functions (Buggert et al., 2014; Doering et al., 2012; Paley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased expression of Eomes in conjunction with PD-1/PD-L1 may characterize anergized CD8+ T cells induced after CD3 Ab therapy.
source: In our transplant model, as detailed below, the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway is mandatory for CD8 T cell tolerance. Thus, increased expression of Eomes in conjunction with PD-1/PD-L1 may characterize anergized CD8+ T cells induced after CD3 Ab therapy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing both Eomes upregulation and PD-1/PD-L1 expression in tolerant CD8+ T cells.

claim: Chronic antigenic stimulation delivers signals inducing a preferential and sustained expression of Eomes.
source: Lastly, one important feature common to our model and the infectious setting is the continuous presence of the cognate antigens. Therefore, we may hypothesize that chronic antigenic stimulation delivers signals inducing a preferential and sustained expression of Eomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that both chronic infection and the transplant model involve continuous antigen presence.

claim: The PD-1/PD-L1 pathway played a predominant role in the induction and the maintenance phase of CD3 Ab-mediated tolerance.
source: The PD-1/PD-L1 pathway played a predominant role in the induction and the maintenance phase of CD3 Ab-mediated tolerance as neutralization of either receptor completely abrogated the therapeutic effect.
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data showing rejection when PD-1 or PD-L1 were blocked.

claim: The PD-1/PD-L1 signaling was mandatory for CD8+ T cell unresponsiveness.
source: More precisely, we demonstrated that the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling was mandatory for CD8+ T cell unresponsiveness.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that blocking PD-1/PD-L1 restored CD8+ T cell effector functions.

claim: In vivo administration of anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies restored the effector functions of allogeneic CD8+ T cells.
source: In vivo administration of anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies restored the effector functions of allogeneic CD8+ T cells, as shown by the up-regulation of the proliferation marker Ki67 and the IFNγ transcription factor T-bet as well as the regained ability to secrete IFNγ, and resulted in islet allograft rejection.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and functional data.

claim: PD-1 has been identified as a marker of dysfunctional CD8+ T cells in various settings.
source: In various settings, PD-1 has been identified as a marker of dysfunctional CD8+ T cells, and it contributed to the establishment of tolerance (Barber et al., 2006; Haspot et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2005; Lucas et al., 2011; Riella et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PD-L1 can interact with B7-1 aside from PD-1.
source: In addition, aside from PD-1, PD-L1 can interact with B7-1 and a recent report demonstrated that this interaction contributed to the control of allogeneic T cell responses (Keir et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction between PD-L1 and B7-1 contributed to the control of allogeneic T cell responses.
source: In addition, aside from PD-1, PD-L1 can interact with B7-1 and a recent report demonstrated that this interaction contributed to the control of allogeneic T cell responses (Keir et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PD-L1 engagement on graft-infiltrating CD8+ T cells may deliver inhibitory signals.
source: We can thus hypothesize that PD-L1 engagement on graft-infiltrating CD8+ T cells may deliver inhibitory signals and that these bidirectional interactions may promote and sustain T cell anergy and graft survival.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that CD8+ T cells co-express PD-1 and PD-L1.

claim: Bidirectional interactions involving PD-L1 may promote and sustain T cell anergy and graft survival.
source: We can thus hypothesize that PD-L1 engagement on graft-infiltrating CD8+ T cells may deliver inhibitory signals and that these bidirectional interactions may promote and sustain T cell anergy and graft survival.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing PD-1/PD-L1 co-expression.

claim: CD3 antibodies cured type 1 diabetes and restored self-tolerance in a TGFβ-dependent manner.
source: We have previously shown in autoimmunity that CD3 antibodies cured type 1 diabetes and restored self-tolerance in a TGFβ-dependent manner (Belghith et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: TGFβ signaling in T cells is mandatory for the induction of immune tolerance by CD3 Ab treatment.
source: Secondly, we demonstrated that TGFβ signaling in T cells is mandatory for the induction of immune tolerance as CD3 Ab treatment failed to induce long-term islet graft survival in recipients presenting a T cell-selective mutated TGFβRII (Gorelik and Flavell, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by graft survival data in DnTGFβRII transgenic mice.

claim: TGFβ has an in situ autocrine/paracrine effect on allogeneic T cells.
source: This result argues for an in situ autocrine/paracrine effect of TGFβ on allogeneic T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that TGFβ is produced by intragraft T cells and that T cell-specific TGFβRII signaling is required for tolerance.

claim: CD3 Ab-induced PD-L1 expression on CD8+ T cells was highly dependent on TGFβ/TGFβR signaling.
source: This inhibitory effect was even more drastic on PD-L1 than PD-1 showing that CD3 Ab-induced PD-L1 expression on CD8+ T cells was highly dependent on TGFβ/TGFβR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that TGFβ blockade more drastically reduced PD-L1 than PD-1 expression.

claim: Tolerance was established through elimination of highly cytotoxic CD8+ T cells followed by the induction of CD8+ T cells anergy.
source: In conclusion, our study highlighted new facets of immune mechanisms driving CD8+ T cell peripheral tolerance and permanent acceptance of fully mismatched allografts after CD3 Ab therapy. Tolerance was established through elimination of highly cytotoxic CD8+ T cells followed by the induction of CD8+ T cells anergy which depended on a cross-talk between the PD-1/PD-L1 and TGFβ/TGFβRII pathways acting in an autocrine and paracrine manner in the graft environment.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD3 Ab have shown potential value in the treatment of patients with new onset type 1 diabetes.
source: These mechanistic findings support the therapeutic potential of CD3 Ab which, concerning clinical translation, have shown potential value in the treatment of patients with new onset type 1 diabetes (Herold et al., 2002; Keymeulen et al., 2005; Sherry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.
